title: Permissions (E1)
scopeHtml: Scope: permission types, runtime request flow, denial semantics, location/notification/media permissions, special access, revocation, manifest and custom permissions, and permission-driven production incidents (API 23 to 34+).

questions.promptHtml: Explain normal, dangerous, signature and special permissions in Android. How does the system decide which are granted at install time and which need the user?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know there is no single "permission dialog" model, and which kind needs which code path.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Every permission has a protection level. Normal ones, like INTERNET, are low risk and granted automatically at install. Dangerous ones, like CAMERA or ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, touch private data, so since API 23 the app must ask at runtime and the user can revoke later. Signature permissions are granted only if my app is signed with the same certificate as the app that declared the permission. Special permissions, like SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW or SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM, are not requested with a dialog at all; the user flips a toggle on a dedicated Settings screen.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each permission is declared by the platform or by an app with android:protectionLevel. The package installer reads <uses-permission> and decides per level.

Level Granted when How app obtains it Examples
normal Install time, automatic Declare in manifest only INTERNET, ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE, VIBRATE
dangerous (runtime) User approves at runtime (API 23+) Declare + request CAMERA, RECORD_AUDIO, READ_CONTACTS, ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, POST_NOTIFICATIONS (API 33)
signature Same signing cert as declarer Declare, system checks cert custom IPC permission between your own apps
special / app-op User toggles on a Settings page Send an Intent to the Settings page, then re-check SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, WRITE_SETTINGS, MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM, PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS

Runtime permissions are grouped (for example the LOCATION group). Since API 26, granting one permission in a group does not grant the others, but a later request for another permission in an already-granted group is auto-approved with no dialog. Never rely on grouping; request exactly what you need and check each permission individually.

If an app targets API 22 or lower, the old install-time model applies on API 23+ devices too, but the user can still revoke in Settings, and the app then gets empty or default data instead of an exception. That legacy path is why very old targetSdk apps behave strangely.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android">
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />            <!-- normal -->
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.CAMERA" />              <!-- dangerous -->
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW" /> <!-- special -->
</manifest>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking that declaring a dangerous permission in the manifest is enough on API 23+. It only makes the app eligible to ask.
  • Calling requestPermissions for a special permission. It does nothing useful; you must launch the Settings intent.
  • Treating the permission group as a promise. A group member you did not declare is not granted.
  • Forgetting that signature permissions silently fail when debug and release signing certs differ.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you check what a permission's level is? → adb shell pm list permissions -f -g, or the PermissionInfo.protectionLevel API.
  2. What is a "restricted" permission? → Sensitive permissions (SMS, call log) that only the default handler app or specially exempted apps can hold; also governed by Play policy.
  3. What changes for a signature permission when I use a different build variant? → Different signing cert means the grant is refused; this breaks cross-app IPC between debug and release builds.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer lists "normal and dangerous". The senior answer adds signature and special/app-op permissions, explains that each has a different request path, and names the Play policy layer on top for restricted permissions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team shipped an overlay feature using requestPermissions(SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW) and never saw a dialog; the fix was Settings.ACTION_MANAGE_OVERLAY_PERMISSION plus a re-check in onResume.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the correct way to request a runtime permission today. Why did the Activity Result API replace onRequestPermissionsResult?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The request flow is the most common permission code; the signal is whether you know lifecycle-safe registration and process-death behavior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I check checkSelfPermission first; if granted I proceed. Otherwise I launch a request through a contract registered with registerForActivityResult(RequestPermission()). The result lands in a callback, not in a request-code switch. Registration must happen before the owner is STARTED, typically as a property initializer, and the registry restores the callback after process death.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Old way: ActivityCompat.requestPermissions(activity, perms, requestCode) plus onRequestPermissionsResult. Problems: integer request codes collide, the result is routed through the Activity even when the request came from a Fragment, and logic is split between two places.

New way: ActivityResultRegistry (activity 1.2+, fragment 1.3+) maps a string key (derived from a counter or an explicit key) to a contract and a callback. Launching sends an Intent to the system GrantPermissionsActivity (PermissionController); when the user answers, the registry dispatches to your callback.

property init (before STARTED) -> registry.register(key, contract, callback)
click -> launcher.launch(CAMERA)
          -> system PermissionController dialog (separate task)
          -> result Intent -> registry -> your lambda
Process death while dialog is open:
          -> activity recreated -> register() with same key again -> pending result delivered

If the app asks for multiple permissions, RequestMultiplePermissions() returns Map<String, Boolean>. Dialogs are queued one after another by the system. A request for an already-granted permission returns immediately granted without UI.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class CameraFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_camera) {
    private val requestCamera =
        registerForActivityResult(ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()) { granted ->
            if (granted) startCamera() else showCameraDenied()
        }

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        view.findViewById<View>(R.id.capture).setOnClickListener {
            val ok = ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(
                requireContext(), Manifest.permission.CAMERA
            ) == PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED
            if (ok) startCamera() else requestCamera.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling registerForActivityResult inside a click listener or after STARTED. It throws IllegalStateException: LifecycleOwner ... is attempting to register while current state is RESUMED.
  • Requesting inside onResume unconditionally; after a denial the screen loops through dialogs.
  • Assuming the result arrives synchronously or that the Activity is not recreated while the dialog is open.
  • Mixing legacy requestCode handling with new contracts in the same screen.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a Fragment need its own launcher? → Yes, register in the Fragment; the result is delivered to it, not to the host Activity.
  2. What happens if a permission is already granted when I call launch? → The system returns immediately with granted; no UI.
  3. How do you test it without UI? → Use GrantPermissionRule, or inject a fake ActivityResultRegistry through registerForActivityResult(contract, registry, callback).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows the API. Senior explains registration timing, why keys survive process death, and how to inject a registry for tests.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash cluster "attempting to register while current state is RESUMED" appeared after a refactor moved registration into a button handler.

questions.promptHtml: How do shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() and "don't ask again" actually work, especially on Android 11+? How do you detect that a permission is permanently denied?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: There is no direct API for "permanently denied". Candidates who rely on the method naively ship dead-end flows.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale returns false before the first ask, true after one denial, and false again once the system will no longer show the dialog. On Android 11+, a second denial for the same permission acts as "don't ask again", and later launch() calls return denied instantly with no dialog. To detect permanent denial I combine: result denied AND rationale false AND I have asked before, which I track myself.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
State machine for one permission:

never asked   : granted=false, rationale=false   -> request shows dialog
denied once   : granted=false, rationale=true    -> request shows dialog (explain first)
denied twice  : granted=false, rationale=false   -> request returns denied immediately, no UI (API 30+)
user-fixed in Settings: granted=true

Before API 30, users had an explicit "Don't ask again" checkbox on the second dialog. On API 30+ the checkbox is gone; two denials produce the same effect. Dismissing the dialog by tapping outside or Back counts as a denial on newer releases. Do not hardcode "twice"; the docs describe it as repeated denial, and behavior can change by release.

The rationale method also returns false when the permission is granted, or when a device policy forbids the user from granting it. So "false" alone is ambiguous: this is why you need your own "has asked" flag (in a ViewModel or SharedPreferences) to separate "never asked" from "permanently denied".

Practical detection:

private fun state(activity: Activity, perm: String, askedBefore: Boolean): PermState = when {
    ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(activity, perm) == PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED -> PermState.Granted
    ActivityCompat.shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(activity, perm) -> PermState.ShowRationale
    askedBefore -> PermState.PermanentlyDenied
    else -> PermState.NeverAsked
}

When permanently denied, the only route is Settings.ACTION_APPLICATION_DETAILS_SETTINGS with Uri.fromParts("package", packageName, null).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating rationale == false after a denial as always meaning permanent denial, then showing a Settings button when it was a never-asked state on first launch.
  • Showing a rationale dialog before every request, which doubles friction.
  • Not re-checking permission in onResume after the user returns from Settings.
  • Persisting "asked before" across reinstall or auto-reset; auto-reset returns the state to never asked.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale work from a Fragment? → Use shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() on the Fragment, which delegates to the host.
  2. Does the user pressing "Ask every time" change anything? → That choice (location, camera, mic) means each launch shows the dialog; the permission is not left granted.
  3. How do you handle the permanently denied state in UX? → Explain the benefit, offer a degraded path, and deep-link to Settings with an in-app explanation; never loop dialogs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "rationale tells you if the user clicked don't ask again". Senior explains the ambiguity, tracks "asked" state, and knows the API 30 semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An onboarding flow looped forever on Android 11 devices because it called launch() repeatedly after the second denial and nothing ever came back except instant false.

questions.promptHtml: What changed for location permissions in Android 12 (API 31), and how should an app request ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION and ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Location is the most scrutinized permission; request-shape mistakes silently fail.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: From API 31, the user can choose "Approximate" or "Precise" on the dialog. An app targeting 31+ that wants precise must request COARSE and FINE together in one request; asking only for FINE is ignored. The user may grant only approximate, so I must work with coarse accuracy and ask for upgrade only when the feature truly needs it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Android 12 dialog has two toggles: Precise and Approximate, then While using / Only this time / Don't allow. Approximate location is a fuzzed position of roughly a few square kilometers (check the docs for current numbers); it comes from ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION and is what the user gets if they choose approximate even though FINE is declared.

Rules for targetSdk 31+:

  • Declare both permissions in the manifest if you may need precise.
  • Request FINE alone and the system ignores the request and logs an error.
  • You can request COARSE alone if approximate is enough.
  • If the user granted only approximate, a later request for FINE shows the dialog again, once; this is an upgrade ask.
  • Check by testing both: FINE granted means precise, COARSE granted but FINE not means approximate.
request [COARSE]            -> dialog offers approximate only
request [COARSE, FINE]      -> dialog offers precise or approximate
request [FINE]  (target 31) -> ignored, logged

Apps targeting below 31 still run on Android 12: if they request only FINE, the system adds the choice and the app must handle getting only coarse.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private val locationLauncher = registerForActivityResult(
    ActivityResultContracts.RequestMultiplePermissions()
) { result ->
    val fine = result[Manifest.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION] == true
    val coarse = result[Manifest.permission.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION] == true
    when {
        fine -> startPreciseTracking()
        coarse -> startApproximateMode()
        else -> showDenied()
    }
}

fun ask() = locationLauncher.launch(
    arrayOf(Manifest.permission.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION, Manifest.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION)
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Requesting FINE only on target 31+, then seeing no dialog.
  • Assuming granted COARSE means "less accurate but still good enough for turn-by-turn". It is not.
  • Ignoring that the user can downgrade from precise to approximate later in Settings.
  • Using the permission check as a proxy for the Location Services toggle; the system location switch is separate.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A weather app, a ride-hailing app and a store locator: which permission? → Weather: coarse. Ride-hailing: fine. Store locator: coarse first, optional upgrade.
  2. How do you detect that the user downgraded after granting? → Re-check both permissions at every use point.
  3. Does FusedLocationProvider hide this? → It respects the grant; priority PRIORITY_HIGH_ACCURACY with only coarse grant returns coarse-quality fixes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE requests FINE and calls it done. Senior designs for coarse as the default, justifies precise per feature, and handles runtime downgrade.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After targeting 31, a delivery app's driver map showed positions off by blocks for users who tapped Approximate, and support tickets blamed "GPS bugs".

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate's QR scanner screen crashes in 1.4% of sessions on first launch, and a QA note says "after denying camera, the app keeps showing the dialog and the screen is black". Android 13 and 14 devices only. Code:

class ScanActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private lateinit var cameraLauncher: ActivityResultLauncher<String>

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_scan)
        findViewById<Button>(R.id.start).setOnClickListener {
            cameraLauncher = registerForActivityResult(ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()) { granted ->
                startCamera()
            }
            cameraLauncher.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)
        }
    }

    override fun onResume() {
        super.onResume()
        if (checkSelfPermission(Manifest.permission.CAMERA) != PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED) {
            requestPermissions(arrayOf(Manifest.permission.CAMERA), 7)
        }
    }

    private fun startCamera() { /* opens CameraX */ }
}

Logcat excerpt: java.lang.IllegalStateException: LifecycleOwner ScanActivity is attempting to register while current state is RESUMED. LifecycleOwners must call register before they are STARTED.
questions.promptHtml: Find every bug, explain why each causes the symptoms, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Move register to onCreate" and stop. Misses the result ignored (granted unused), the dialog loop from onResume, and that two request mechanisms are mixed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the crash on first tap or on later taps? (registration per click). Does the black screen follow a denial? (granted flag ignored). Is it reproducible with Do-not-keep-activities? (registry callback timing).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; a small hotfix is acceptable: gate the crash by moving registration out of the click.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) registration in a click handler throws once the Activity is RESUMED, (b) startCamera() runs even when denied, (c) onResume re-requests on every resume so a denial redisplays, and the system dialog's pause/resume cycle re-triggers it, (d) the legacy requestPermissions has no matching onRequestPermissionsResult.
  4. How I'd verify each: Read the stack trace for (a); add logs for granted; adb shell pm revoke <pkg> android.permission.CAMERA then launch; background/foreground the app to trace onResume loops.
  5. Root cause: Registration after STARTED; result discarded; two mechanisms and an unguarded onResume request.
  6. Fix:
class ScanActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val cameraLauncher = registerForActivityResult(
        ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()
    ) { granted -> if (granted) startCamera() else showDeniedState() }

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_scan)
        findViewById<Button>(R.id.start).setOnClickListener { ensureCamera() }
    }

    private fun ensureCamera() {
        if (checkSelfPermission(Manifest.permission.CAMERA) == PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED) startCamera()
        else cameraLauncher.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Lint check for registerForActivityResult inside lambdas; unit test with a fake registry; checklist: "register in property init, request only from user action".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not catch the IllegalStateException; that hides the lifecycle bug. I would not request in onResume unconditionally.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the user wants auto-start without a button? → Request once in onStart guarded by a requested flag saved in savedInstanceState.
  • The result is false; what UI? → Rationale state or Settings deep link based on Q291 state machine.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A scanner screen passed QA because testers always had permission pre-granted via adb install -g. Real users hit the denied path and the loop; the fix was a denied-state UI plus a test run with permissions revoked.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Fixes only the exception; still ignores the result.
  • Hire: Finds registration timing, ignored result, and onResume loop; writes the corrected version.
  • Strong hire: Also explains why -g hid it, adds revoked-permission test coverage, and covers denial state design.

questions.promptHtml: What are one-time permissions and permission auto-reset? How do they affect an app that assumes "granted once means granted forever"?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These features silently break background work in the field. Seniors design for permission loss as normal.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Android 11 added "Only this time" for location, camera and microphone. The grant lasts while the app is in use and is revoked after the app leaves the foreground for a while or its process dies. Separately, auto-reset revokes runtime permissions of apps the user has not used for several months. In both cases the app must re-check at the point of use and be ready to ask again.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
One-time (API 30): the grant is tied to the user's session with the app. Once the app has been in the background for a grace period, or the process ends, the system revokes it. A foreground service that started while the permission was valid can continue for a short time; do not depend on that. After revoke, checkSelfPermission returns denied, and shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale returns false, but the dialog can be shown again because the user did not choose a permanent denial.

Auto-reset (Android 11+ for apps targeting API 30+; Google Play services backport to Android 6 to 10): after an app is unused for several months, the system resets runtime permissions and may hibernate the app (stops background work, clears caches). Apps can ask the user to exempt them: Intent.ACTION_AUTO_REVOKE_PERMISSIONS, and PackageManagerCompat.getUnusedAppRestrictionsStatus() to read the status, IntentCompat.createManageUnusedAppRestrictionsIntent() to open the toggle.

Consequences:

  • Permission state is not durable app state. Never cache granted = true in preferences.
  • Background jobs (WorkManager, FCM-triggered) must check permission at execution time and fail gracefully, for example by posting a "tap to re-enable" notification.
  • Analytics: a drop in "permission granted" can be due to auto-reset rather than user choices.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun hasLocation(ctx: Context) =
    ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(ctx, Manifest.permission.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION) ==
        PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED

// In background worker:
if (!hasLocation(applicationContext)) return Result.failure() // and surface a re-enable prompt

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Persisting a "location enabled" flag instead of re-checking.
  • Assuming a foreground service keeps a one-time grant forever.
  • Not testing the revoked-in-background path; adb shell pm revoke simulates it.
  • Asking for exemption from hibernation without explaining why.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you simulate auto-reset? → adb shell cmd app_hibernation set-state <pkg> true and adb shell pm reset-permissions variants (verify availability per release).
  2. Does one-time apply to every dangerous permission? → No, only location, camera, microphone.
  3. How should a long-running tracker behave? → Use a foreground service with proper type and permission; if revoked, stop cleanly and notify the user.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows the "Only this time" button. Senior ties it to background work, hibernation, and tests revocation as a first-class path.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fitness app's morning sync silently stopped for lapsed users because auto-reset removed location permission and the worker threw SecurityException.

questions.promptHtml: How does the notification runtime permission in Android 13 work, and how does behavior differ for apps targeting 32 vs 33 or higher?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It affects engagement metrics for almost every app and has subtle targetSdk-dependent behavior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: POST_NOTIFICATIONS is a dangerous permission from API 33. If I target 33+, I must declare it and request it myself; until granted, my notifications are not shown. If I target 32 or lower, the system prompts the user automatically the first time I create a notification channel while an activity is in the foreground. I should ask in context, after a moment of value, not at cold start.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cases on an Android 13+ device:

App New install Updated from pre-13 OS
targets 33+, permission declared Notifications blocked until user grants. App calls the request Existing notification-enabled apps keep notifying (grandfathered)
targets 32 or lower System shows the prompt when the app first creates a channel with a foreground activity Same grandfathering

Details worth knowing:

  • Without a declared POST_NOTIFICATIONS in the manifest, an app targeting 33+ cannot get the prompt; requestPermission just returns denied.
  • Foreground service notifications are displayed in the Task Manager even if the user denied the permission, but the notification itself may not appear in the drawer.
  • Two denials follow the usual permanent-denial rule (Q291).
  • NotificationManagerCompat.areNotificationsEnabled() covers app-level state across all API levels, while per-channel importance is separate (NotificationChannel.importance == IMPORTANCE_NONE).
  • The system dialog appears only when the app has created at least one channel.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private val notifLauncher = registerForActivityResult(
    ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()
) { granted -> viewModel.onNotificationPermission(granted) }

fun maybeAskForNotifications(ctx: Context) {
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 33 &&
        ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(ctx, Manifest.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS)
            != PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED
    ) notifLauncher.launch(Manifest.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the manifest declaration after bumping targetSdk to 33; users see nothing and the request does nothing.
  • Prompting on first launch before the user sees any benefit.
  • Using only checkSelfPermission and ignoring channel-level or Do-Not-Disturb states.
  • Not building an in-app fallback (badge, inbox) for users who deny.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can an app targeting 32 still get a prompt on Android 13? → The platform shows it automatically on first channel creation; there is no app control over timing.
  2. How to ask again after one denial? → Show rationale UI then launch; after the second denial send the user to ACTION_APP_NOTIFICATION_SETTINGS.
  3. How to measure impact? → Funnel: eligible installs, prompt shown, granted, notification delivered; compare by API level cohort.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "request POST_NOTIFICATIONS". Senior explains targetSdk-dependent behavior, grandfathering, prompt-timing strategy, and fallback channels.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A targetSdk 33 bump shipped without the manifest line; push opt-in on Android 13 devices dropped to near zero for a week.

questions.promptHtml: How did media access permissions change across Android 10, 13 and 14, and why is the photo picker the preferred answer for most apps?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Storage permission is a long-running pain. The signal is whether you pick the lowest-privilege API instead of asking for broad access.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If the user just needs to choose photos or videos, I use the photo picker and need no permission at all. Android 13 split READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE into READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, READ_MEDIA_VIDEO and READ_MEDIA_AUDIO. Android 14 added READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED so the user can grant access to only chosen items, which means I must treat "partial access" as a normal state.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Timeline:

API Change
29/30 Scoped storage: apps see their own files plus MediaStore contributions; READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE for others' media
33 For apps targeting 33+, READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE has no effect; use READ_MEDIA_IMAGES/VIDEO/AUDIO
34 READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED: user may pick "Select photos and videos" (partial)
Any Photo picker (ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia) needs no permission

Photo picker is a system UI that returns content URIs for the selected items; your app gets temporary read access to exactly those. It works on Android 11+ via system updates, and PickVisualMedia falls back to the Google Play services picker or ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT on older devices (check current support matrix on developer.android.com). Use PickMultipleVisualMedia(maxItems) for multi-select.

Partial access on API 34: declare READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, READ_MEDIA_VIDEO and READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED, request all in one call. Possible outcomes:

  • Full access: READ_MEDIA_IMAGES granted.
  • Partial: READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED granted, READ_MEDIA_IMAGES denied. Your MediaStore queries return only chosen items.
  • None. Do not assume the selection persists forever; re-check at each launch, and offer "choose more" via a new request. Also note that Google Play restricts broad READ_MEDIA_IMAGES/VIDEO to apps whose core purpose needs it (gallery, editors); verify the current policy before shipping.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val pickMedia = registerForActivityResult(ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia()) { uri ->
    if (uri != null) loadImage(uri)   // temporary read access granted to this URI
}
pickMedia.launch(PickVisualMediaRequest(ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia.ImageOnly))
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_MEDIA_IMAGES" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE" android:maxSdkVersion="32" />

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Declaring READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE only and wondering why nothing works on 33+.
  • Treating READ_MEDIA_IMAGES denied as "no access" on 34 when partial access is granted.
  • Persisting a picker URI without takePersistableUriPermission when using OPEN_DOCUMENT; picker URIs are temporary.
  • Requesting audio permission for an image-only feature.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the picker work for documents? → No, use SAF (ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT) for arbitrary files.
  2. How do I read the file? → contentResolver.openInputStream(uri); do not convert to a path.
  3. How do I keep access across restarts? → Copy into app storage, or use SAF with persistable permissions; picker URIs may expire with the process.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE requests READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE or READ_MEDIA_IMAGES. Senior avoids the permission via the picker, handles partial access on 14, and considers the Play policy review risk.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After targeting 34, an upload feature failed for users who chose "Select photos" because code checked READ_MEDIA_IMAGES only.

questions.contextHtml: A 1.5M DAU expense-tracking app has a "scan receipt" flow that requires CAMERA. Analytics: 31% of users deny on first ask; of those, 55% tap the button again and see nothing happen. Support reports "camera is broken". On Android 11+, the second denial blocks future dialogs. A PM wants to "keep asking until they accept". Android 11 to 14 are 70% of the base.
questions.promptHtml: How would you redesign the flow, and what would you tell the PM?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Keep calling requestPermissions" or "show a Toast saying permission denied". Both are dead ends and the first literally cannot work after permanent denial.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is camera the only way to enter a receipt? (alternatives). How many receipts come from gallery already? What is the denial count by OS version? Is the permission needed for the whole app or only that flow? (scope). Are there enterprise-managed devices with camera disabled?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Replace the silent tap with a denied-state screen that explains why and offers two actions: "Open Settings" and "Pick from gallery".
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) permanent denial after two attempts causes silent failure, (b) users deny because the ask came before they understood the benefit, (c) camera hardware absent or disabled by policy, (d) OEM dialog differences.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log the Q291 state (NeverAsked/ShowRationale/PermanentlyDenied) with the tap; segment by OS version; reproduce with adb shell pm revoke twice; check PackageManager.hasSystemFeature(FEATURE_CAMERA_ANY).
  5. Root cause: The code treats the permission as a gate with only a request path; there is no state machine for denial.
  6. Fix: Use the state machine: NeverAsked -> show a one-line value prop then request; ShowRationale -> explain then request; PermanentlyDenied -> show inline panel with Settings deep link and gallery alternative. Also offer MediaStore.ACTION_IMAGE_CAPTURE, which uses the system camera app and needs no CAMERA permission if the app does not declare it (if the app declares CAMERA, the intent path requires the grant, so choose based on product need). Re-check in onResume after returning from Settings.
  7. Prevention: Test matrix includes "denied twice" on API 30+; analytics for each state; UI test with revoked permission.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not loop the dialog or hide the feature; I would not request all permissions at startup. Gallery fallback loses live scan quality but keeps 100% of users functional.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• PM says "can we detect permanent denial earlier?" → No API tells you; I track asked-state myself and treat rationale false after an ask as permanent.
  • User allowed "Only this time" yesterday and is back today: what do I show? → Treat it as NeverAsked again; ask in context.
  • Enterprise device disables camera: → hasSystemFeature can be true while a policy blocks use; catch CameraAccessException and show a policy message.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team lifted completion of the flow from 69% to 88% by shipping a gallery fallback and explaining value before the first ask, with no change to the permission itself.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests repeating the request.
  • Hire: Builds a state machine, Settings deep link, and alternative path.
  • Strong hire: Adds metrics per state, hardware/policy edge cases, and the product-vs-privacy trade-off argument to the PM.

questions.promptHtml: How do special permissions like SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW and SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM differ from runtime permissions, and how do you request and check them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many developers wrongly use requestPermissions for these; also exact alarms changed twice in recent releases.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Special permissions are controlled by app ops and a dedicated Settings screen, not by a system dialog. I launch an Intent to the relevant screen, the user toggles, and I re-check on return, since there is no result callback with the answer. SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW uses Settings.canDrawOverlays; exact alarms use AlarmManager.canScheduleExactAlarms().

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Key special permissions and their checks:

Permission Check Settings intent
SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW Settings.canDrawOverlays(ctx) ACTION_MANAGE_OVERLAY_PERMISSION + package: URI
WRITE_SETTINGS Settings.System.canWrite(ctx) ACTION_MANAGE_WRITE_SETTINGS
MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE Environment.isExternalStorageManager() ACTION_MANAGE_APP_ALL_FILES_ACCESS_PERMISSION
SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM AlarmManager.canScheduleExactAlarms() (API 31+) ACTION_REQUEST_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM
REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES packageManager.canRequestPackageInstalls() ACTION_MANAGE_UNKNOWN_APP_SOURCES

Exact alarms timeline: introduced in API 31, pre-granted for apps through Android 13 behavior; from Android 14, newly installed apps targeting 33+ have it denied by default (apps updated from earlier versions keep their grant). USE_EXACT_ALARM (API 33) is auto-granted and cannot be revoked, but Play policy limits it to alarm-clock, timer and calendar apps. When the user revokes SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM the app is killed and its exact alarms canceled; the system sends ACTION_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION_STATE_CHANGED when it is granted again, so reschedule from a receiver. Deeper alarm and Doze behavior belongs to the Doze chunk.

Overlay specifics: TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY replaced legacy window types in API 26; on Android 12+, untrusted touches passing through overlays are blocked unless the overlay is mostly transparent (verify exact alpha rule in docs).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun ensureExactAlarm(activity: Activity) {
    val am = activity.getSystemService(AlarmManager::class.java)
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 31 && !am.canScheduleExactAlarms()) {
        activity.startActivity(Intent(Settings.ACTION_REQUEST_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM,
            Uri.parse("package:${activity.packageName}")))
    }
}
// re-check in onResume; there is no result callback with the answer

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling canScheduleExactAlarms() on API 30 and below; it exists from 31.
  • Assuming the grant is permanent; the user can revoke, killing the process.
  • Using startActivityForResult and trusting the result code.
  • Requesting USE_EXACT_ALARM for a feature that is not alarm/calendar, then failing Play review.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do I know if I can use inexact instead? → If the feature tolerates a window of minutes, setAndAllowWhileIdle avoids the permission.
  2. What happens to scheduled exact alarms when permission is revoked? → They are removed and the app is killed.
  3. Why does MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE trigger store review? → It gives all-files access; Play allows it only for narrow use cases.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows the Settings intent. Senior knows the version-dependent defaults, receiver for re-grant, and policy alternatives.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reminder app's alarms stopped on new installs on Android 14 because the grant default flipped to denied.

questions.promptHtml: A third-party SDK adds permissions you never asked for through manifest merging. How do you find, remove and control them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Libraries silently expand your permission surface, causing Play rejections, privacy-policy violations and install friction.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The manifest merger unions every <uses-permission> from all AARs into the final APK. I inspect the merged manifest, remove what I do not need with tools:node="remove", narrow with maxSdkVersion, and mark hardware features as required="false" so Play does not filter devices out.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Merge order, lowest to highest priority: library manifests, then build-type/flavor manifests, then main manifest. Permissions are additive; the merger never drops one on its own.

Inspection:

  • Android Studio: Merged Manifest tab shows each permission and its source.
  • CLI: ./gradlew :app:processReleaseMainManifest then read app/build/intermediates/merged_manifests/release/.../AndroidManifest.xml; or inspect an APK/AAB with apkanalyzer manifest permissions app.apk or aapt2 dump permissions app.apk.

Control:

<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools">
    <!-- remove a permission some SDK added -->
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_PHONE_STATE" tools:node="remove" />
    <!-- legacy permission needed only on old OS -->
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE" android:maxSdkVersion="28" />
    <!-- do not exclude phones without the hardware -->
    <uses-feature android:name="android.hardware.camera" android:required="false" />
</manifest>

Why uses-feature: declaring a permission such as CAMERA can imply a required hardware feature, causing Play to filter out devices without it unless you declare required="false".

Risks of removing: the SDK may crash or degrade if it expects the permission; read its docs and check checkSelfPermission usage. Also review that removal does not affect <queries> or <provider> entries.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fixing the debug manifest and forgetting release; always inspect the release merged manifest.
  • Removing a permission an SDK uses at runtime without checking the failure mode.
  • Missing implicit features: Play listings show device exclusions.
  • Putting maxSdkVersion on a permission that is still needed on newer APIs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you prevent regressions? → CI step diffing aapt2 dump permissions against a committed allowlist.
  2. Is tools:node="removeAll" useful? → Rarely; it removes every matching element; use targeted removal.
  3. Where do tools:node="merge" conflicts show up? → In the merge report; with tools:replace you override attribute values.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE adds tools:node="remove". Senior builds a CI guard, understands implied features, and weighs SDK behavior after removal.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A release was blocked by Play for a "Phone state" permission added by an ad SDK update that nobody read in the diff.

questions.contextHtml: A smart-lock companion app (400k MAU) bumps targetSdk from 30 to 34. Within 48 hours, support tickets say "cannot find my lock" and Crashlytics shows a new top crash, 0.9% of sessions, all on Android 12 and above: java.lang.SecurityException: Need android.permission.BLUETOOTH_SCAN permission for AttributionSource{...}: GattService startScan Android 11 and below users are fine. The manifest still declares BLUETOOTH, BLUETOOTH_ADMIN and ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION; the code checks only location permission before scanning. Red herrings: a BLE library update shipped the same day, and one OEM reports slow scans.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix, and explain how you would ship it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll back the library" or "ask for location permission again". The first ignores the log; the second is the pre-12 requirement.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did crash rate correlate with OS version and targetSdk bump or with the library? Is there a pairing flow that also connects (CONNECT)? Do we advertise anywhere? What is the minimum supported OS?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix that wraps scan start in a permission check and shows "Allow Nearby devices" instead of crashing; staged rollout from 10%.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) targetSdk 31+ requires BLUETOOTH_SCAN, BLUETOOTH_CONNECT (and ADVERTISE) at runtime on Android 12+, (b) library regression, (c) location services toggle off, (d) OEM scan throttling.
  4. How I'd verify each: The exception text names BLUETOOTH_SCAN (settles a). Compare crash rates before/after the library bump on API 30 devices (rules out b). adb shell pm revoke BLUETOOTH_SCAN and reproduce. Review merged manifest.
  5. Root cause: Android 12 split Bluetooth access into the "Nearby devices" runtime group. Apps targeting 31+ must hold BLUETOOTH_SCAN to scan and BLUETOOTH_CONNECT to connect; legacy BLUETOOTH/BLUETOOTH_ADMIN only apply to API 30 and below.
  6. Fix:
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BLUETOOTH" android:maxSdkVersion="30" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BLUETOOTH_ADMIN" android:maxSdkVersion="30" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION" android:maxSdkVersion="30" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BLUETOOTH_SCAN"
    android:usesPermissionFlags="neverForLocation" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BLUETOOTH_CONNECT" />
val required = if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 31)
    arrayOf(Manifest.permission.BLUETOOTH_SCAN, Manifest.permission.BLUETOOTH_CONNECT)
else arrayOf(Manifest.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION)

neverForLocation lets Android 12+ skip the location requirement if we do not derive location from scans; it filters out some beacon results, so verify the lock's advertising packets still appear. 7. Prevention: Behavior-change checklist in targetSdk bumps; instrumented test on API 31+ emulators with permissions revoked; pre-merge manifest diff. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not stay on targetSdk 30 (Play requires recent targets). I would not request location on 12+ when neverForLocation suffices.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just keep ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION on 12+? → It still works for location use, but without neverForLocation scanning also needs location services on in some cases; it adds a needless prompt.
  • Android 13 Wi-Fi scanning? → NEARBY_WIFI_DEVICES replaces location for Wi-Fi peer discovery.
  • Why still need Location Services on API 30? → Pre-12, scan results are location-sensitive, so the system requires the location toggle.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A hardware team found the fix only on the third day because the crash was filtered by "new SDK version" instead of OS version; a one-line breakdown by Build.VERSION.SDK_INT would have shown the pattern in minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames the library; cannot explain the permission split.
  • Hire: Identifies BLUETOOTH_SCAN/CONNECT, fixes manifest and runtime request by API level.
  • Strong hire: Explains neverForLocation trade-off, staged rollout, and a targetSdk bump checklist.

questions.contextHtml: Your Espresso/UI Automator suite has 420 tests and runs on CI emulators (API 30, 33 and 34). Flake rate is 6%, and the top failing tests are anything involving the camera, location or notifications. Failures: UiObjectNotFoundException: no object with text "While using the app". Different API levels and one OEM-skinned device farm show different button labels. Total run time is 48 minutes, a third of which is permission dialog handling.
questions.promptHtml: How do you stabilize and speed this up without losing coverage of the permission flows?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add Thread.sleep" or "retry failed tests 3 times", which hides bugs and increases CI cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which tests actually test permission handling vs just need the permission? Are we using Test Orchestrator and clearing data? Is the dialog being driven by text selectors or resource IDs? Which devices are the flakiest?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Quarantine the 8 worst tests behind a flag and pre-grant permissions for tests that only need them.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) text-based selectors differ by version and locale, (b) race between the app's request and dialog appearance, (c) leftover grants across tests without clearPackageData, (d) animation/IME interference.
  4. How I'd verify each: Capture screenshots and adb shell uiautomator dump at failure; run with adb shell settings put global window_animation_scale 0; log pre/post permission states with dumpsys package <pkg> | grep -A20 "runtime permissions".
  5. Root cause: Tests drive a system UI that is not stable across OS versions or OEMs, and they pay for that UI in every test, not just the ones that need it.
  6. Fix:
  • Split: most tests use @get:Rule val perm = GrantPermissionRule.grant(Manifest.permission.CAMERA); only a small, dedicated set exercises the dialog.
  • For dialog tests, select by resource id (for example com.android.permissioncontroller:id/permission_allow_foreground_only_button) with fallback, verified per API level; IDs differ on some OEMs.
  • Use adb shell pm grant/pm revoke in setup, and pm reset-permissions between tests.
  • Make the permission request injectable (fake ActivityResultRegistry) so the app's reaction to granted/denied is unit-tested without any system UI.
  1. Prevention: Test Orchestrator with clearPackageData; a small "permission matrix" job on one fixed API image; track flake rate per test.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add sleeps or blanket retries. I would not skip the real-dialog tests entirely; keep a few on a pinned emulator image so version shifts are caught.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Device farm OEM dialogs differ: → Do not automate OEM dialogs; pre-grant via pm grant there and cover dialog flows on stock images.
  • Time dropped to 31 minutes but the denied flow was untested: → Add a revoked-state test via the fake registry.
  • GrantPermissionRule does not work for special permissions: → Use appops set <pkg> <op> allow or settings commands in setup.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Splitting "needs permission" from "tests permission UI" cut a suite from 55 to 29 minutes and removed 80% of flaky reruns.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds sleeps and retries.
  • Hire: Uses GrantPermissionRule and pm grant/revoke, isolates real-dialog tests.
  • Strong hire: Adds injectable registry, orchestrator isolation, special-permission app ops, and flake metrics.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the two-step flow for background location (ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION), how it differs across API 29, 30 and 31+, and when you can avoid it.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It combines permission mechanics, UX, Play policy and foreground services. Senior engineers must know how to avoid needing it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Background location is a separate permission added in API 29. On API 30+, I cannot request it together with foreground location; I must first get foreground permission, then separately request background, and the system sends the user to Settings to choose "Allow all the time" rather than showing a dialog. Most use cases (tracking during a run, navigation) can use a foreground service with a location type and avoid the background permission altogether.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Behavior by version:

API Request behavior
29 Background permission shown as a dialog option, could be combined
30+ Cannot request with foreground; the request redirects to the Settings page for the app; no result callback with the answer other than re-check
31+ Approximate/precise options (Q292) apply on top; foreground services started from the background are restricted

Foreground location (the "while using" grant) works when the app has a visible activity or a running foreground service of type location (API 29 requires the manifest foregroundServiceType="location"; Android 14 requires type declaration and matching FOREGROUND_SERVICE_LOCATION permission). That covers a user-visible tracking session without ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION.

You need background location only for work that continues with no user-visible session: geofencing that triggers while the app is not running, passive background collection, and similar. Google Play requires a declaration and review for this permission and rejects apps where a foreground service would do.

Flow:

foreground request (COARSE/FINE) -> granted
explain why "all the time" needed -> user taps
launch request(ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION) -> (API 30+) opens Settings page
user selects "Allow all the time" -> onResume -> re-check

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private fun requestBackground(activity: Activity) {
    // only after foreground location is granted
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 29) {
        backgroundLauncher.launch(Manifest.permission.ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION)
    }
}
// On 30+ this sends the user to Settings; re-check in onResume
override fun onResume() {
    super.onResume()
    viewModel.refreshBackgroundGranted(
        ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(this, Manifest.permission.ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION)
            == PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED
    )
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Including background in a RequestMultiplePermissions call on API 30+; it is ignored.
  • Assuming checkSelfPermission for foreground grants covers a background service.
  • Not providing the Play declaration video and justification.
  • Treating "While using the app" as enough for geofencing triggers when the app is not in use.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a foreground service replace it? → Yes for user-initiated sessions; location type FGS keeps foreground-level access.
  2. How does Android 12 limit starting such a service from the background? → Foreground service starts from background are blocked with exemptions; see the Services chunk.
  3. What about battery? → Background location use is also reported in system privacy dashboard (Android 12+), which can alarm users.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE asks for both together. Senior avoids the need through foreground services, handles the Settings redirection, and manages Play policy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fitness app was rejected twice by Play review because its justification described a feature a foreground service already covered.

questions.promptHtml: What happens to your app when the user revokes a runtime permission in system Settings while the app is running or in the background? How should you design for it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Revocation is a state change the app does not initiate. It exposes cached-permission bugs and process-death assumptions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Permission state lives in the system, not in my app. Historically, revoking a runtime permission from Settings kills the app's process, so the user returns to a recreated process and an Activity restored from saved state. Behavior varies by permission and release (some app-op based permissions can change without a kill), so I never cache "granted", I check at the point of use, and I handle SecurityException as a possible outcome.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Revoke path: Settings -> PermissionController -> PermissionManagerService updates the grant and, for runtime permissions, typically ends the app's process so any state keyed to the old grant (native handles, gids) is dropped. Treat the kill as likely but not guaranteed; docs do not promise a specific mechanism. Do not hardcode it.

What the user sees after a kill:

App in recents -> user taps it
   -> new process, Application.onCreate runs
   -> Activity recreated from savedInstanceState (back stack preserved)
   -> ViewModels are NEW (ViewModelStore died with the process)
   -> singletons/static fields reset

Design consequences:

  • Do not cache permission state in static fields, singletons, or savedInstanceState; they may be restored as true after revocation.
  • Request-or-check in onStart/onResume, or before each use.
  • Guard permission-annotated APIs (@RequiresPermission) with a check and a try/catch for SecurityException for races (revoked between check and call).
  • Long-lived consumers (location callbacks, camera sessions, FGS) need a stop path when permission disappears; for FGS the system can end the service when the process is killed.
  • Persist intent ("user wanted tracking on"), not capability; on restore, re-verify capability.

For special permissions like exact alarms the revoke kills the process and cancels alarms (Q298).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onStart() {
    super.onStart()
    val granted = ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(
        this, Manifest.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION
    ) == PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED
    if (viewModel.trackingWanted && granted) startUpdates() else stopUpdatesAndPrompt()
}

private fun startUpdates() = try {
    fused.requestLocationUpdates(request, callback, Looper.getMainLooper())
} catch (e: SecurityException) {   // revoked between check and call
    stopUpdatesAndPrompt()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saving hasPermission in onSaveInstanceState; it is restored and wrong after revocation.
  • Checking once at login and storing the result in a singleton.
  • Catching SecurityException and swallowing it with no user-visible state.
  • Testing only with the app in the foreground; adb shell pm revoke while backgrounded reveals the restore path.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does granting also restart the app? → Generally no, only revoking is disruptive; on old releases storage grants had side effects.
  2. How do you test? → Revoke via adb shell pm revoke <pkg> <perm>, then open from recents; also use "Don't keep activities".
  3. How does it interact with ViewModel? → ViewModel state is lost on a kill; restore intent via SavedStateHandle and re-verify capability.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "the app crashes if you don't check". Senior says revocation is a process-death event, separates intent from capability, and checks at use time.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tracking screen saved "permission granted" in its saved state; after revocation and kill, it resumed and crashed on the first location call (see Q304).

questions.contextHtml: A running-tracker app (900k DAU) sees a new crash on Android 12 to 14: 0.42% of sessions, mostly "resume from recents". Stack: java.lang.SecurityException: uid 10456 does not have android.permission.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION or android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION at com.google.android.gms.location.FusedLocationProviderClient.requestLocationUpdates called from TrackFragment.onStart. Facts: crash volume spiked after a "Privacy Dashboard" campaign by a phone vendor. The app was launched with Play services 24.x; QA cannot reproduce because testers grant location once on a fresh install. A red herring: the same release updated the maps SDK.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: cause, fix, prevention, and what changed in your process.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in try/catch and ship." That removes the crash while the user sees a blank tracker and no way to fix it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the app in the background at the time of revocation? Does the crash happen only in onStart after process recreation? Does the crash rate correlate with "location revoked" events? Does the Fragment restore a tracking=true flag?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-flagged hotfix to guard onStart; staged rollout; add a remote kill switch for the auto-resume behavior.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) user revoked in Settings, process was killed, saved state says tracking, onStart starts updates without checking; (b) one-time permission expired (Q294); (c) auto-reset after months unused; (d) maps SDK regression.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce: start tracking, background, adb shell pm revoke <pkg> android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION (also COARSE), reopen from recents. Check Crashlytics keys: time since last foreground, savedState presence, API level. Correlate crash count with Android privacy dashboard campaign timing. Rule out (d) by bisecting the SDK bump.
  5. Root cause: Fragment persisted capability (tracking=true implied permission) and ran requestLocationUpdates in onStart after the system revoked permission and recreated the process.
  6. Fix: Short term: check before start and catch SecurityException, moving UI into a "Location needed" state with a button for the request/Settings flow. Long term: persist user intent only; a PermissionState flow derived from checkSelfPermission on every onStart; a single LocationSource wrapper that exposes Flow<Result> and converts SecurityException into PermissionLost.
override fun onStart() {
    super.onStart()
    viewModel.onScreenStart(hasLocationPermission(requireContext()))
}
  1. Prevention: Add a QA scenario "revoke in settings while backgrounded"; lint/code-review rule: no permission booleans in saved state or singletons; Crashlytics custom key for permission state; alert on any new SecurityException.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not auto-prompt on every onStart (annoying); show state and let the user act. I would not request background location to keep tracking alive; use the foreground service model.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• It happens inside a foreground service: → The service may have been killed with the process; on restart, check permission before startForeground location work.
  • Crash only on Samsung: → Check vendor permission UIs that set "allowed only while using" and the Doze/battery interplay; still guard at use.
  • How do you quantify success? → SecurityException rate to ~0 and funnel metric for "permission lost" recovery.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team found that 70% of the crashes came from users who had the app open in a split-screen next to Settings; adding revoke-in-background to the test script exposed it in two minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds try/catch and closes the ticket.
  • Hire: Identifies revoke -> kill -> restore with stale state, adds check + UI state.
  • Strong hire: Separates intent from capability, adds repro commands, metrics, and process-level prevention.

questions.promptHtml: When would you define a custom permission, and how do protection levels, exported components and android:permission fit together? What attacks exist if you get it wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Inter-app and component security is a senior concern; mis-set permissions are a classic audit finding.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A custom permission lets me gate access to my exported components, such as a service or provider, so only trusted callers can use them. I choose signature when only my own apps (same signing cert) should have access, since the system enforces the cert match and the user never sees a prompt. A normal custom permission is nearly useless as protection because any app can request it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Declare and protect:

<permission
    android:name="com.example.suite.permission.SYNC"
    android:protectionLevel="signature" />

<service
    android:name=".SyncService"
    android:exported="true"
    android:permission="com.example.suite.permission.SYNC" />

<uses-permission android:name="com.example.suite.permission.SYNC" />

When another process calls into the service, the system checks that the caller holds the permission before onBind is delivered. For provider per-URI access and grantUriPermissions, see the Providers chunk.

Protection levels and use:

Level Use
normal Almost never; not a security boundary
dangerous Rare for custom; user is asked; avoid
signature Same-cert app suite; strongest and simplest
signature with additional flags (privileged/preinstalled) OEM and system apps only

Attack surface:

  • Missing android:permission on an exported component: any app can invoke it.
  • Permission squatting: a malicious app declares your permission name first with a weaker level. Mitigated since API 21 (second declaration from a different signer fails install), but name collisions in your own app family when installation order varies still matter; always use package-prefixed names.
  • Confused deputy: your exported component performs privileged actions on caller-supplied Intents (intent redirection). Validate; do not forward raw Intents.
  • Caller identity: Binder.getCallingUid() and checkCallingPermission() are used for fine-grained checks inside the component; for AIDL services check on each call.

Debug vs release signing breaks signature permissions between apps; keep the same keystore in test flavors or provide a separate debug permission.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• exported="true" without any permission or validation.
  • Using normal for a "secret" permission.
  • Forgetting <uses-permission> in the caller; the call fails with SecurityException.
  • Checking getCallingUid() after clearing the calling identity with clearCallingIdentity().

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you check the caller inside an AIDL method? → enforceCallingPermission or checkCallingPermission on the Context; compare Binder.getCallingUid() to expected package signature when needed.
  2. Why prefer signature over app allowlists by package name? → Package names are spoofable pre-install; the signing cert is not.
  3. How do you rotate keys? → APK Signature Scheme v3 key rotation lineage; plan for it before shipping a suite.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows android:permission. Senior reasons about protection levels, caller identity, signing and attack classes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A pen test flagged an exported sync service with a normal custom permission; any app could trigger uploads of local data.

questions.subtopic: checkSelfPermission vs PermissionChecker and app ops
questions.promptHtml: What's the difference between ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission and PermissionChecker.checkSelfPermission, and why can a permission be "granted" but the access still fail?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests deep understanding of the two-layer model: permission grant plus app-op mode.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A runtime permission has a grant state, and many are also tied to an app-op that the system uses to track and restrict usage, such as "while in use" location or the user turning off a permission for background. checkSelfPermission reports only the grant. PermissionChecker also consults the app op and can return PERMISSION_DENIED_APP_OP. For foreground-only location, checkSelfPermission says granted even when my app is in the background and the system will not deliver real data.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two layers:

Layer 1: permission grant (granted/denied)         -> ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission
Layer 2: app-op mode (allow / foreground / ignored / errored)
         + context (foreground? attribution? hibernated?) -> actual access

PermissionChecker.checkSelfPermission(context, permission) returns one of PERMISSION_GRANTED, PERMISSION_DENIED, or PERMISSION_DENIED_APP_OP. Use checkPermission variants with a package name and uid when checking on behalf of a caller (for example in a provider, with attribution). Beyond that:

  • Foreground-only location grant: Layer 1 says granted; background delivery fails or returns nothing because the op mode is "foreground".
  • Notification permission: use NotificationManagerCompat.areNotificationsEnabled(), not only checkSelfPermission (Q295).
  • Camera/microphone toggles (API 31 privacy toggles): the system can block access globally; sensors return empty or CameraAccessException, regardless of grant.
  • Hibernated apps: grants reset (Q294).

Inside a service answering IPC callers, checking your own permission is not what you want; use checkCallingPermission or PermissionChecker.checkCallingPermission, which uses the caller's identity. Be careful about Binder.clearCallingIdentity() before such checks.

Implication: "granted" is never proof that the next call will succeed. Combine a check for UI with defensive handling for failure, and surface "no data" states instead of crashing.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val result = PermissionChecker.checkSelfPermission(ctx, Manifest.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION)
when (result) {
    PermissionChecker.PERMISSION_GRANTED -> start()
    PermissionChecker.PERMISSION_DENIED_APP_OP -> showAppOpBlocked()
    else -> requestPermission()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming GRANTED means the app can collect location while backgrounded.
  • Using checkSelfPermission inside a provider to validate callers; it validates your own process.
  • Confusing PERMISSION_DENIED_APP_OP with a normal denial; the request dialog may not fix it.
  • Forgetting sensor privacy toggles (mic/camera) when diagnosing empty audio.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is attribution tag for? → Lets a library or feature separate its accesses in the privacy dashboard; use createAttributionContext() (API 30+).
  2. How do you inspect app ops? → adb shell appops get <pkg> and adb shell dumpsys package <pkg>.
  3. How does a content provider check callers? → checkCallingOrSelfPermission / enforceCallingPermission plus manifest readPermission/writePermission.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE treats the check as truth. Senior knows the second layer and writes code assuming access can fail even when granted.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A background sync reported "location granted" in diagnostics but delivered no fixes for "only while in use" users; the root cause was app-op mode, not the grant.

questions.contextHtml: A commerce app with 2M DAU targets SDK 32 today and must move to 33 (store requirement in 6 weeks). About 38% of users are on Android 13+. Currently on Android 13 the system prompt appears automatically at first channel creation (cold start), with 72% opt-in. Marketing says "push drives 30% of orders; do not lose reach". Product also says "we want a nicer prompt, but no more than one extra screen". The requirement is ambiguous on whether existing users should be re-prompted.
questions.promptHtml: Plan the targetSdk 33 migration and the permission strategy, and tell me what you'd measure.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add POST_NOTIFICATIONS and call launch on app start." This loses the grandfathering knowledge, the timing control, and the denial flow.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What counts as success: opt-in rate or orders from push? Are there transactional notifications (order status) that matter more than promotional? Can we segment by intent? Do we have an in-app inbox? Does the target date allow an experiment first?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; first ship the manifest line and the code path behind a flag, with a default that reproduces today's behavior (request on first session).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) contextual timing after a value moment (first order, wishlist) beats cold start; (b) priming screen helps only if the system prompt follows immediately; (c) existing users on 13 are grandfathered and need no prompt; (d) new installs after bump with no request get zero notifications.
  4. How I'd verify each: A/B on new installs: cold start vs post-first-order, measuring granted rate and 7-day push-attributed orders; guardrails on D1 retention. Confirm grandfathering by testing an upgrade on a physical Android 13 device and an emulator.
  5. Root cause: Behavior depends on targetSdk: below 33 the platform controls the prompt; at 33+ the app must ask, so timing and denial recovery become product features.
  6. Fix: Declare POST_NOTIFICATIONS; request after a value moment with one sentence of context; after a denial, never auto-reprompt, instead show a persistent in-app banner leading to ACTION_APP_NOTIFICATION_SETTINGS; keep transactional notifications on their own high-importance channel so users can keep them while muting promos.
  7. Prevention: Funnel dashboards by API level, alert on opt-in drops, regression test in the targetSdk checklist, and a fallback inbox.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not re-prompt existing users who already have notifications working. I would not ask at cold start just to keep the old number; I accept a lower early rate in exchange for better quality and long-term retention, validated with data.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Marketing wants a prompt every launch: → The system limits dialogs after two denials; spamming leads to permanent denial and uninstalls.
  • Opt-in dropped from 72% to 55% in the experiment: → Check if the control used the same moment; test priming plus later contextual asks, and weigh order impact, not opt-in alone.
  • Users on Android 12 and lower: → No runtime permission; notifications on by default.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shop moved the ask from cold start to the order-confirmation screen. Opt-in fell a little, but push-attributed orders per opted-in user rose because users knew why they allowed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds the permission call at startup.
  • Hire: Knows targetSdk-dependent behavior, grandfathering, denial handling.
  • Strong hire: Frames experiments, guardrails, channel strategy, and negotiates the ambiguous requirement.

questions.contextHtml: A document-scanner app (3M MAU, 20% on Android 10 or lower) targets SDK 29, uses WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE with requestLegacyExternalStorage="true", and saves PDFs to /sdcard/ScanPro/. Play requires targetSdk 34 next quarter. Test builds on API 33 show FileNotFoundException: open failed: EACCES on old files, and a user-reported missing-files complaint appeared in the beta channel. Constraints: no data loss, exports must stay visible in the Files app, the app may not ask for MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE.
questions.promptHtml: Design the migration plan.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Request MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE" (policy risk), or "just use getExternalFilesDir" (files vanish on uninstall and are not visible to the user).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which files must be shareable and survive uninstall? Do other apps read /sdcard/ScanPro/? What is the file count per user (p95)? Do we write only PDFs or also images? Is there cloud backup already?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Before bumping the target, ship a release at target 29 or 30 that migrates data while the app still has legacy access.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) requestLegacyExternalStorage is ignored for apps targeting 30+, so old files become inaccessible; (b) on upgrade, preserveLegacyExternalStorage (set on a build targeting 29 or 30) keeps access until uninstall on Android 11; (c) other apps read the path.
  4. How I'd verify each: Test installs of old build upgraded to new on API 29, 30, 33 and 34 emulators; adb shell ls -l /sdcard/ScanPro; dump dumpsys package for storage flags; run a migration unit test.
  5. Root cause: Scoped storage (enforced for target 30+) blocks raw path access to shared storage for non-media files and makes WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE ineffective.
  6. Fix:
  • New writes: MediaStore.Downloads (API 29+) with RELATIVE_PATH = "Download/ScanPro" and IS_PENDING while writing; for API 28 and lower, keep WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE with maxSdkVersion="28".
  • Optional user-chosen folder: SAF (ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT_TREE) with persisted permission.
  • Migration: while still holding legacy access (a transitional release), copy existing files into MediaStore or app-specific storage, verify checksums, then delete originals; run it as a resumable background job with progress and retries.
val values = ContentValues().apply {
    put(MediaStore.Downloads.DISPLAY_NAME, "scan_001.pdf")
    put(MediaStore.Downloads.MIME_TYPE, "application/pdf")
    put(MediaStore.Downloads.RELATIVE_PATH, "Download/ScanPro")
    put(MediaStore.Downloads.IS_PENDING, 1)
}
val uri = resolver.insert(MediaStore.Downloads.EXTERNAL_CONTENT_URI, values)!!
resolver.openOutputStream(uri)!!.use { out -> writePdf(out) }
resolver.update(uri, ContentValues().apply { put(MediaStore.Downloads.IS_PENDING, 0) }, null, null)
  1. Prevention: Staged rollout (1%, 10%, 50%), telemetry on migration success, file count before/after, support playbook; keep a rollback path (do not delete originals until verified).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE (Play restricts it to a narrow set of apps). I would not skip the transitional release, since users who never open the app in that window lose easy access to old files.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• User never updates through the transitional release: → Provide an in-app "recover old files" flow using SAF folder pick of /sdcard/ScanPro once.
  • Files must be readable by a partner app: → Share via MediaStore or FileProvider/SAF; no raw path.
  • Reinstall after uninstall: → Legacy-location files are only visible via SAF or MediaStore ownership rules; user-created files by the old install may not be owned by the new one.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team lost trust when a rushed target bump hid users' old exports; a resumable copy job with checksums and a "recover" screen contained the damage within a week.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE or ignores existing user data.
  • Hire: Uses MediaStore/SAF, adds a transitional migration release.
  • Strong hire: Addresses ownership, upgrade/reinstall edge cases, staged rollout, verification and rollback.
